provisions.title: Standard of consent
provisions.text: (1) The consent given by the Data Principal shall be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action, and shall signify an agreement to the processing of her personal data for the specified purpose and be limited to such personal data as is necessary for such specified purpose.

provisions.title: Exposure of Sensitive Information Due to Incompatible Policies
provisions.text: The product's intended functionality exposes information to certain actors in accordance with the developer's security policy, but this information is regarded as sensitive according to the intended security policies of other stakeholders.

provisions.title: Broken Object Level Authorization
provisions.text: Every API endpoint that receives an ID of an object, and performs any action on the object, should implement object-level authorization checks. The checks should validate that the logged-in user has permissions to perform the requested action on the requested object.

negative

value.reason: At routes/changePassword.ts:45 the code loads the full User record with UserModel.findByPk(loggedInUser.data.id). No attributes list is passed, so nothing narrows which fields are fetched. At line 56 it sends the whole instance back with res.json({ user }). Per models/user.ts, the User model holds more than profile data: the hashed password (set via security.hash), several redacted secret-like string fields (likely things like a TOTP secret or deluxe token), lastLoginIp, role and profileImage. Nothing in the evidence shows a toJSON override, a defaultScope, attribute filtering or a response DTO that would remove these fields before sending. The response therefore exposes the password hash and other internal or sensitive properties the client doesn't need after a password change. This matches the positive example (findByPk, then res.json({ user }) with no attribute restriction) and is excessive data exposure at the object-property level. The record is the caller's own, chosen by the session user id rather than a request parameter, so this is not object-level authorization (API1). It is still an over-exposure of sensitive properties and a failure to put reasonable safeguards on personal data.
